newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Highlights of South Korea's new labour law.
newsitem.headline: Highlights of South Korea's new labour law.

text.p: A new labour bill adopted by the South Korean parliament sparked a nationwide strike by workers fearful that decades of job security is coming to an end.
The government argues that flexible labour practices are needed to maintain the country's industrial competitiveness, and will secure jobs in the long run.
Here are the controversial points in the new bill:
-- Companies may lay off workers made surplus by structural changes, technical innovation and changes in their business.
-- Employers may replace striking workers with their own staff or outside workers on a temporary basis. Companies may sub-contract work during a strike.
-- Striking workers will not be paid.
-- Flexible work hours may be introduced up to a maximum 56-hour working week.
-- Unions may join political activities, including fund raising for political parties and candidates.

-- Multiple unions will be allowed from 2000. The Korean Federation of Labour Unions is now the sole umbrella organisation recognised by the government. The smaller and more militant Korean Confederation of Labour Unions will remain illegal until 2000.
-- Salaries to all full-time union officers will be phased out by 2002.
